title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / St...
summary: Windows starts programs at sign in from a small set of registry values and from two Startup folders. The Run and RunOnce values exist separately for the current user and for the local machine, with a Wow6432Node copy for 32-bit code, and the machine-wide RunOnceEx key can load a library through its Depend subkey rather than launching an executable. Legacy RunServices and RunServicesOnce values, the Explorer Run policy keys, the load value under the Windows NT key and the BootExecute value under Session Manager offer further autostart points, and the Explorer Shell Folders keys can even move the Startup folder itself. Anything placed in these locations runs in the context of the signing-in user with that account's rights. The artefacts are registry writes to those values, files or shortcut files appearing in a Startup folder, and process creation shortly after a logon where the parent is the shell or the logon initialiser. Very many legitimate updaters and hardware utilities use Run keys, so a baseline, a signature check and a look at the file path matter far more than the mere presence of an entry.

beginner.definition: This technique adds a program to a list that Windows reads when a user signs in. Windows keeps these lists in the registry and in two Startup folders. One folder belongs to a single user, and the other applies to everyone. Anything in those places starts automatically at sign in. An attacker adds their program to one of them, so it returns after every restart. This sub-technique is one part of the parent idea about starting code when the system or a user begins a session.
beginner.whyItMatters: This is one of the simplest ways to keep a program running on a Windows computer. The program starts with the user's own rights, so nothing unusual appears in the security log at first glance. Many real programs use the same lists, so an attacker's entry can hide among them. If you never compare the lists with a known good state, unwanted software can return after every cleanup.
howItWorks: Windows has a few registry keys that list programs to start when a user signs in.
A value under the Run key starts a program at every sign in, and RunOnce runs it only once.
Some of these keys belong to one user, and others apply to every user of the machine.
The Startup folder does the same job, because any program or shortcut inside it runs at sign in.
An attacker adds an entry that points to their file, and the entry returns after each restart.
Attackers may also edit the registry values that tell Windows where the Startup folder is kept.
beginner.example: Think of a flat where a note by the front door says on the way out, switch on the hall light. Everyone follows it without thinking. If someone adds and unlock the shed, the first flatmate to leave does that too, every single morning. Run keys and the Startup folder are that note. Windows reads them at every sign in and starts whatever they name.
takeaways: Run, RunOnce and the Startup folders start programs at sign in with the user's rights.
Legitimate software uses these places too, so check the file path and its signature.
Attackers can also move the Startup folder by editing the Explorer Shell Folders keys.

objectives: Name the registry keys and folders that start programs at sign in.
Explain the difference between Run and RunOnce, and between user and machine scope.
Describe the RunOnceEx Depend method that loads a library instead of a program.
Identify telemetry for registry writes and for processes started soon after logon.
Explain how the Startup folder location itself can be redirected.
Distinguish a legitimate autostart entry from an attacker's one.
